verses.1: For the music director. A testimony for Asaph. A psalm.
verses.2: Sing joyfully to our God, Israel, sing to the God of Jacob.
verses.3: Play a song, beat the tambourim, with a pleasant lyre and a harp.
verses.4: Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, in our festival time.
verses.5: For it is a law for Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob.
verses.6: He set it as a testimony in Joseph, when he brought him out from the land of Egypt, a language he had not known, which he heard.
verses.7: I removed the burden from his shoulder, his hands were freed from the plow.
verses.8: In trouble you called to me, and I rescued you. I heard your voice in the hidden storm, I tested you on the waters of Meribah — Selah.
verses.9: Listen, my people, and I will speak to you, Israel, and I will bear witness to you. If you would only listen to me!
verses.10: There shall be no strange god among you, and you shall not bow to a foreign god.
verses.11: I am the LORD, your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.
verses.12: But my people did not listen to my voice, and Israel did not want me.
verses.13: So I let them go on the desires of their hearts, they walked in their own counsel.
verses.14: If only the people had listened to me, Israel had walked in my ways,
verses.15: I would have quickly subdued their enemies, and on those who oppressed them, I would have laid my hand.
verses.16: Those who hate the LORD would have been deceitful to him, and their time would have been forever.
verses.17: And I would have fed them with the fat of wheat, and with honey from the flint I would have satisfied them.

notes:
Notes  
- v. 8: "tested you on the waters of Meribah" — "Meribah" is a known site of contention (e.g., Exodus 17:7). The Hebrew word "Selah" is retained as a musical or liturgical marker.  
- v. 13: "the desires of their hearts" — the Hebrew uses "mo'adot" (plans), which is rendered here in context as "desires of their hearts."  
- v. 10: "strange god" / "foreign god" — the Hebrew uses "el zar" and "el nechar," translated directly to avoid ambiguity.  
- v. 17: "flint" — the Hebrew "tzur" can mean "rock" or "flint," and the context of honey from rock is preserved.

Notes  
- v. 8: "tested you on the waters of Meribah" — "Meribah" is a known site of contention (e.g., Exodus 17:7). The Hebrew word "Selah" is retained as a musical or liturgical marker.  
- v. 13: "the desires of their hearts" — the Hebrew uses "mo'adot" (plans), which is rendered here in context as "desires of their hearts."  
- v. 10: "strange god" / "foreign god" — the Hebrew uses "el zar" and "el nechar," translated directly to avoid ambiguity.
